title: Equivalences between pattern-fibered objects detected over base edges
statement:
Use categorical patterns, marked objects over $\bar C$, and $\mathfrak P$-fibered objects from [def-coef-categorical-pattern-fibrancy], marked products from [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], categorical equivalences of simplicial sets from [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure], and weak homotopy equivalences from [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Let $\mathfrak P=(C,S,\{p_\alpha\})$ be any small fully scaled pattern, and let $f:X\to Y$ be a map of $\mathfrak P$-fibered marked objects over $\bar C$. Put $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(A,Z)_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{/\bar C}(A\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp,Z)$. The following are equivalent:

(1) For every $\mathfrak P$-fibered $Z$, restriction $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(Y,Z)\to\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(X,Z)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

(2) For every edge $e:\Delta^1\to C$, including degenerate edges and edges outside $S$, the induced underlying simplicial map $X\times_C\Delta^1\to Y\times_C\Delta^1$ is a categorical equivalence.

The objects in (2) are quasicategories. There is no assumption that every edge of $C$ lies in $S$, and (2) does not assert that vertex fibers alone suffice.

source.place: Higher Algebra, Lemma B.2.4, equivalence (1) with (3), printed pp.1483-1485. Its vertex-only variant is not used. Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this infinity-categorical result.

proof.text: Write condition (1) as the P-equivalence mapping test. By [lem-coef-pattern-anodyne-lifting-products], every sharp mapping simplicial set into a P-fibered target is Kan, and restriction along a cofibration is a Kan fibration. If f has a map g:Y→X and marked homotopies gf≃id_X and fg≃id_Y over C, precomposition by g is a homotopy inverse to precomposition by f on every sharp mapping complex, so (1) holds. Conversely, apply (1) with Z=X and Z=Y: surjectivity on π₀ supplies g with gf connected to id_X, and injectivity on π₀, applied after composing with f, supplies a homotopy fg≃id_Y. Kan fillers combine finite edge paths into single sharp Δ¹-homotopies. Thus (1) is equivalent to the homotopy-inverse condition in Higher Algebra Lemma B.2.4(2).

source.place: Lemma B.2.4, formal equivalence of (1) and (2), printed p.1483.

proof.text: Restrict the marked homotopy inverse from Step 1 along any $e:\Delta^1\to C$. Put $E=X\times_C\Delta^1$ and $F=Y\times_C\Delta^1$. Pullback of inner horn lifting shows that $E,F$ are quasicategories by clause (i) of [def-coef-categorical-pattern-fibrancy]. A component of either pulled-back homotopy is marked, so clause (ii) makes its edge in $X$ or $Y$ cocartesian over a degenerate edge of $C$. Such an edge is an equivalence in its vertex fibre: both it and the identity at its source are initial lifts of that degenerate base edge by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality], and the comparison of these initial lifts gives the edge itself as an equivalence of targets. The inverse triangles remain in the fibre, hence give equivalences also in $E$ or $F$. By [lem-coef-infinity-pointwise-equivalences] the restricted homotopies are natural equivalences of functors. Thus the restricted maps are genuine quasi-inverses, and [lem-coef-joyal-quasicategory-characterizations](2) makes $E\to F$ a categorical equivalence. This proves condition (2) for every edge, whether or not it belongs to $S$.

Assume (2). For any marked $W\to\bar C$, call $W$ good if postcomposition induces a weak homotopy equivalence $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W,X)\to\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W,Y)$. Call an edge $u$ locally cocartesian if $(u,\mathrm{id}_{\Delta^1})$ is cocartesian in the pullback along its base edge. For an edge over $S$, local cocartesianness is equivalent to global cocartesianness. Indeed a global cocartesian edge remains cocartesian on pullback, by its horn lifting property. Conversely choose a global cocartesian lift $v$ with the same source and base edge, using clause (ii) of [def-coef-categorical-pattern-fibrancy]. The local lifts $u,v$ are initial in the same lift quasicategory by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality]; comparison supplies an equivalence between their targets in the vertex fibre and a triangle relating $u$ to $v$. A fibre equivalence is globally cocartesian by [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-mapping-criterion]: its top mapping-space map is an equivalence and its bottom map is the identity. Composition in [lem-coef-infinity-cocartesian-composition-initiality] then makes $u$ globally cocartesian. Consequently the marking in clause (ii) is exactly the locally cocartesian edges over $S$. Over a degenerate base edge it is exactly the fibre equivalences, by the initial-lift argument of Step 2 and the same mapping criterion.

For every base edge $e$, the equivalence $f_e:E\to F$ preserves and reflects cocartesian edges over $\Delta^1$. To see this without a quasi-inverse over the base, apply the mapping criterion to an edge and each target vertex. An equivalence induces equivalences on the two upper mapping spaces: a quasi-inverse induces inverse maps after conjugating endpoints by the components of the two inverse natural equivalences. Naturality identifies their composites with identity maps up to homotopy, using the associative and unital mapping-space composition of [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition]. The lower spaces are unchanged because $f_e$ is strictly over $\Delta^1$. Essential surjectivity covers the remaining targets in $F$: equivalences between targets lie over identities, since $\Delta^1$ has no other equivalences, and postcomposition gives equivalent squares. The homotopy-pullback property is unchanged under these equivalences by [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-pullback-invariance]. Hence an edge of $X$ is locally cocartesian if and only if its image is. Here categorical equivalence has the quasi-inverse meaning supplied by [lem-coef-joyal-quasicategory-characterizations]; no relative quasi-inverse is claimed.

Put $K_Z=\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W^\flat,Z)$ for $Z=X,Y$; these are Kan by [lem-coef-pattern-anodyne-lifting-products]. From the coordinatewise product marking of [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model], its simplices have vertical components marked over degenerate base edges, thus fibre equivalences. For a marked edge $b$ of $W$, each naturality square has these equivalences as vertical sides. Composition and cancellation of cocartesian edges show that the image of $b$ is cocartesian at one endpoint if and only if it is at the other. The same triangles show that all diagonal product edges $(b,i\to j)$ are marked whenever the vertex diagrams preserve the marking. Therefore $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W,Z)$ is exactly the full simplicial subset of $K_Z$ on marking-preserving vertex diagrams, and this subset is a union of connected components. Preservation and reflection just proved say that the selected components in $K_X$ are exactly the inverse image of those in $K_Y$. A weak equivalence $K_X\to K_Y$ restricts to a weak equivalence on these unions (bijection on selected components and the same based homotopy groups). Thus goodness of $W^\flat$ implies goodness of $W$.

Consider a pushout $W'=W\amalg_V V'$ of simplicial sets over $C$, with $V\hookrightarrow W$ degreewise injective. Mapping out, degree by degree with flat markings, gives the strict pullback $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W'^\flat,Z)=\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W^\flat,Z)\times_{\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(V^\flat,Z)}\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(V'^\flat,Z)$, for $Z=X,Y$. The restriction from $W^\flat$ to $V^\flat$ is a Kan fibration by [lem-coef-pattern-anodyne-lifting-products]. Both strict pullbacks therefore represent homotopy pullbacks by [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. If $V^\flat,V'^\flat,W^\flat$ are good, the map between their three mapping-space corners consists of weak equivalences; [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-pullback-invariance] gives an equivalence on the homotopy pullbacks, hence $W'^\flat$ is good. This is the specific three-input implication needed, not a claim about any three corners of the original pushout.

We first justify the zero and one simplex tests. For $e:\Delta^1\to C$ let $E=X\times_C\Delta^1$, $F=Y\times_C\Delta^1$. Their projections to $\Delta^1$ are isofibrations: they are inner fibrations, and every equivalence in $\Delta^1$ is an identity and lifts to an identity. The equivalence $E\to F$ from (2), interpreted by [lem-coef-joyal-quasicategory-characterizations], therefore induces equivalences on vertex fibres by [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-base-change]. This includes the test at any $c\in C$ by taking its degenerate edge and then either endpoint. We have consequently proved that $E_B=X\times_C B\to F_B=Y\times_C B$ is an equivalence over $B$ for every simplex $B=\Delta^0$ or $\Delta^1$, and both projections are isofibrations.

By [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation] (take $\varnothing\hookrightarrow B$), $\operatorname{Fun}(B,E_B)\to\operatorname{Fun}(B,B)$ and its $F$ analogue are isofibrations. Postcomposition with $E_B\to F_B$ is a functor equivalence: postcompose with an ordinary quasi-inverse and its natural equivalences, using [lem-coef-infinity-pointwise-equivalences] to check the induced transformations. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-base-change] to these functors over $\operatorname{Fun}(B,B)$ and the vertex $\mathrm{id}_B$. Their strict fibres, the quasicategories $\operatorname{Sec}_B(E_B)$ and $\operatorname{Sec}_B(F_B)$ of sections, are equivalent. Passing to cores gives an equivalence of spaces: quasi-inverses and their equivalence transformations restrict to the cores, with the mapping-space interpretation in [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model].

These cores are precisely $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(B^\flat,X)$ and $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(B^\flat,Y)$. Indeed an $n$-simplex is a family of sections on $B\times\Delta^n$; the flat marking on $B$ imposes only that the vertical edges be marked. By the marked-equals-fibre-equivalence argument in Step 3 (using clause (ii), initiality and the mapping criterion), this says exactly that the component edges are fibre equivalences. The pointwise criterion identifies them with equivalence edges of the section quasicategory. Concretely, inverse witnesses in $\operatorname{Fun}(B,E_B)$ remain over $\mathrm{id}_B$: $\operatorname{Fun}(B,B)$ is the nerve of a poset for $B=\Delta^0,\Delta^1$, so any simplex whose vertices are all $\mathrm{id}_B$ is constant. This proves the asserted equality of cores, not just an analogy with edge pullbacks. Hence both flat base cases are good, including degenerate $e$ and edges outside $S$.

The flat consecutive-edge spine is now good by successive pushouts at vertices using Step 4. Its underlying inclusion $i:\operatorname{Sp}[n]\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$ is inner anodyne by [lem-cbc-spine-inner-anodyne]. For each boundary inclusion $j:\partial\Delta^m\hookrightarrow\Delta^m$, [lem-coef-inner-anodyne-pushout-product] makes $i\mathbin\square j$ inner anodyne. Thus the inner fibration $Z\to C$ fills every underlying lifting problem for restriction $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C((\Delta^n)^\flat,Z)\to\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(\operatorname{Sp}[n]^\flat,Z)$ against $j$. The resulting lift preserves markings: every marked edge of $(\Delta^n)^\flat\times(\Delta^m)^\sharp$ has constant first coordinate, and every vertex of $\Delta^n$ is in the spine, so every such edge already belongs to the prescribed spine part. Restriction therefore has the right lifting property against all boundary inclusions, including $m=0$, and is a trivial Kan fibration by [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. In the commutative square for $X,Y$, both restrictions and the spine comparison are weak equivalences; two-out-of-three gives the full simplex comparison. Thus every flat simplex is good.

For arbitrary marked objects, define a $\mathfrak P$-equivalence $u:W\to W'$ to mean that precomposition $u^*:\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W',Z)\to\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W,Z)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every $\mathfrak P$-fibered $Z$. In particular the two horizontal precomposition maps for $Z=X$ and $Z=Y$ are weak equivalences. They commute with the vertical postcomposition maps defining goodness. Their common composite is a weak equivalence if and only if either vertical map is, by two-out-of-three in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Thus $W$ is good if and only if $W'$ is good. There is no cofibration hypothesis on $u$, and no Kan-fibration assertion about its restriction maps. If $u$ is pattern-anodyne, both restriction maps are trivial Kan fibrations by [lem-coef-pattern-anodyne-lifting-products], giving the claimed particular case. This also explains the spine passage in Step 5.

source.place: Lemma B.2.4(e), with Example B.2.2, printed p.1484.

proof.text: Good objects are closed under coproducts: mapping out of a coproduct is a product of Kan complexes. For a product of weak equivalences between Kan complexes, components and every based homotopy group are the corresponding products (sphere and interval maps are computed coordinatewise), so the product map is a weak homotopy equivalence. If W has finite dimension, attach its nondegenerate n-simplices to the (n−1)-skeleton by the boundary pushout. The attaching coproduct and the lower skeleton are good by induction, while the coproduct of n-simplices is good by the coproduct closure just proved together with Step 5, which makes every flat simplex $(\Delta^n)^\flat\to\bar C$ good. The pushout descent of Step 4, with $V$ the attaching coproduct, $W$ the coproduct of $n$-simplices and $V'$ the lower skeleton, then proves W^flat good. The empty simplicial set is included as the initial case.

For arbitrary $W\to C$, write $W=\operatorname{colim}_n W^{(n)}$ for its skeletal union. For each simplicial degree $m$, maps $(W^\flat\times(\Delta^m)^\sharp)\to Z$ over $\bar C$ are exactly compatible maps from $((W^{(n)})^\flat\times(\Delta^m)^\sharp)\to Z$: every simplex and every required marked edge occurs at a finite stage, and agreement on overlaps gives a unique simplicial map. This is an elementary strict identity $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C(W^\flat,Z)=\lim_n\operatorname{Map}^\sharp_C((W^{(n)})^\flat,Z)$, compatible with simplicial operators and postcomposition with $f$; it uses no assertion about mapping spaces between functors. The factors are Kan complexes and their restriction maps Kan fibrations by [lem-coef-pattern-anodyne-lifting-products]. By [lem-coef-kan-fibration-tower-limit], the two strict limits for $Z=X,Y$ compute the limits of the corresponding coherent diagrams of spaces, naturally in the map of towers. Each finite skeleton is good by Step 7, so the map of these diagrams is a pointwise equivalence. Limits preserve such equivalences (their universal mapping-space property identifies the same limiting cones after composing with a diagram equivalence). Hence the induced map of strict limits is a weak homotopy equivalence, and $W^\flat$ is good. Step 3 now makes every marked $W$ good. Empty $W$ gives the constant tower of one-point mapping complexes; empty fibres and infinite-dimensional $W$ require no surjectivity on vertices, exactly as allowed by the tower node.

Take W=Y in goodness. The image of id_Y lifts, up to a sharp homotopy, to a map g:Y→X, giving fg≃id_Y. Take W=X. The two maps id_X and gf have the same image after postcomposition with f, because f g f≃f; goodness of X gives gf≃id_X. Thus f has a homotopy inverse, and Step 1 gives condition (1). Combining Steps 1–8 proves the equivalence of (1) and (2), with no replacement of X or Y and no requirement that edges of C lie in S.
